extracted.intended_audience: readers, students, and practitioners of satirical poetry and classical literature (e.g., translators, poets, Horace readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and implicit standards for composing and performing satirical verse (as articulated by Horace in these Satires): what counts as a poet, acceptable freedoms in satire, stylistic habits, moral aims, and poor practices to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: License of satiric poets to brand vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Satiric poets (Eupolis, Cratinus, Aristophanes, Lucilius) freely branded rascals, thieves, adulterers and infamous men with great freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace defends this liberty as an established practice of ancient comedy and satire; however, the defense comes with the caveat that honest men who live clean lives have no cause to fear such poets. The poet's freedom is to expose vice, not to slander the innocent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine poet: genius and greatness of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘To him who has genius, who has a soul of a diviner cast, and a greatness of expression, give the honor of this appellation.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely tagging a verse or writing in a conversational style does not make one a true poet. The distinguishing qualities are an inspired spirit and forceful expression, beyond mere technical correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy vs. true poetry (animated spirit and force)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy may be questioned as a true poem because often it lacks animated spirit and force; it differs from prose principally by measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a work's style and subject lack that 'animated spirit', it may be mere metered prose rather than true poetry. A poem should retain expressive vitality not present in plain prose—even when metrical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of careful composition and revision
rubrics_metrics.description: Lucilius 'flowed muddily' and was verbose, too lazy to endure the fatigue of writing accurately; producing many verses quickly was faulted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sloppy rapid production (e.g., dictating two hundred verses an hour) and verbosity. Good composition requires labor, careful writing, and revision to remove muddiness and unnecessary material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity and modesty in utterance
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet praises being of 'an humble and meek disposition, speaking but seldom, briefly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conciseness is a virtue in both social speech and poetic expression; speaking rarely and briefly is preferable to constant volubility. This is presented as both a personal virtue and an aid to tasteful satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid malicious slander and unprincipled vituperation
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet disclaims being a malicious accuser and condemns 'black malignity' and mere malice as foreign to his writings and mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire should not be motivated by spite. The author distinguishes critiques meant to correct or instruct from baseless backbiting, feigned stories, and gratuitous attacks on absent friends or private matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Didactic aim: expose particular vices to deter others
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace's father instructed him to note each particular vice so that through example he might avoid them; satire serves to preserve traditional morality and keep life and reputation inviolate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One legitimate aim of satiric writing is moral education — to hold up specific vices as warnings. Satire that records and ridicules faults can function as ethical instruction rather than mere entertainment or personal vendetta.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of public recitation and context
rubrics_metrics.description: Many recite their writings in public places (forum, baths) and at unseasonable times; this pleases coxcombs but is poor taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the setting and audience for recitation. Public or indiscriminate recitation (e.g., in the forum or while bathing) can be thoughtless and diminish the poet’s dignity and the work's reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter, word-order, and the 'limbs' of a poem matter
rubrics_metrics.description: If you take away certain pauses and measures, or transpose words in verse, 'you will not discern the limbs of a poet'—the poetic effect is lost under mere rearrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic form (meter, pause, word order) contributes essentially to poetic identity and effect. Surface rearrangements that ignore metrical and rhythmic integrity can strip verses of their poetic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity and credibility over fabricated display
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of those who 'can feign things he never saw'—the satirist contrasts genuine depiction with false boasting or feigned experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain credibility in voice and content; feigning events or qualities undermines authority. Even in satire or performance, authenticity (or plausibly framed fiction) is valued over empty pretense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social restraint: avoid and distrust excessive loquacity
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'babbling' man is predicted to be the ruin of someone; Horace warns to avoid talkative people who reveal secrets, asperse absent friends, or feign accomplishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a social rule relevant to both life and literary circles: associate cautiously with gossips and boastful performers; their conduct and speech habits are antipatterns for tasteful poetic life and public reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuing modest living and moral worth over noble birth
rubrics_metrics.description: True nobility comes from merit and purity of heart rather than illustrious ancestry; a modest life free from burdensome ambition is preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theme and stance guidance for a satirist/poet: foreground moral character, modest pleasures, and human merit rather than social rank. This is both a subject-matter criterion and an ethic for the author's persona.
